claim: Deep ReLU networks exhibit a systematic learning bias toward low-frequency (globally smooth) functions, which the authors name 'spectral bias'; lower frequency components of the target function are learned first.
stance_target: N5: finite neural networks are spectrally biased toward smooth functions
scope_conditions: ReLU networks, synthetic 1D/manifold regression tasks, MNIST
quoted_support: While neural networks can approximate arbitrary functions, we find that they favour low frequency ones – hence they exhibit a bias towards smooth functions – a phenomenon that we called spectral bias.

claim: Increasing network width does help a network fit higher-frequency (jagged) functions, but the effect of width is considerably weaker than the effect of increasing depth.
stance_target: N5 adversarial reading: width reduces the smoothness bias, but only weakly compared to depth -- a genuine tension for a pure width-artifact mechanism story
scope_conditions: Experiment 7: delta-function target with flat all-frequencies spectrum, ablation over depth/width/weight-clip
quoted_support: Fig 16 shows that increasing the width (for fixed depth) also helps, but the effect is considerably weaker (note that the width increases exponentially).

claim: Increasing depth, for fixed width, significantly improves a network's ability to fit higher frequencies -- depth is the dominant knob for reducing spectral bias, not width.
stance_target: N5: which architectural factor (width vs depth) governs the smoothness bias
quoted_support: Fig 15 shows that increasing the depth (for fixed width) significantly improves the network's ability to fit higher frequencies (note that the depth increases linearly).

claim: The lower-frequency components of a trained network are more robust to random parameter perturbations than the higher-frequency components, manifesting the spectral bias in the parameterization itself, not just the learning trajectory.
stance_target: N5: spectral bias is a property of trained finite networks, evidenced two independent ways
quoted_support: We show that the lower frequency components of trained networks are more robust to random parameter perturbations.

claim: Rahaman et al. never discuss ensembles, Bayesian posteriors, surrogate models, acquisition functions, infinite-width limits, or the neural tangent kernel -- the paper is a single-network supervised-learning Fourier-analysis study.
stance_target: N5/N6: scope boundary of the spectral-bias paper relative to offline-MBO ensemble/surrogate claims
scope_conditions: Full-text grep of extracted PDF (2135 lines)
